articles.title: I gave my smart home its own DNS and finally stopped my privacy settings from breaking it
articles.author: Yadullah Abidi
articles.content:
I have a network-wide privacy setup for my home network that works beautifully until it doesn't. Pi-hole blocked trackers on my laptops and phones, but the same aggressive lists periodically break smart TVs, delay camera notifications, or leave a cloud-dependent bulb hanging off the internet.
This left me in a loop of allowing one mysterious hostname, testing again, and repeating until the device came back online. So I decided to give my smart-home network its own DNS policy, and the constant tug-of-war disappeared overnight.
Pi-hole blocks everything, including your smart bulb's will to live
Your phone can show an error, your bulb just silently gives up
The problem wasn't DNS blocking itself. DNS-level filters are excellent for devices that cannot run browser extensions or privacy apps, as a resolver can refuse to return an address for a tracking or malicious domain, stopping the connection before it starts. Pi-hole and AdGuard Home apply this protection across a network without requiring client software, which makes them rather useful when it comes to IoT devices.
That said, you'll run into problems if you use one blanket policy for every device. My phone can tolerate strict blocklists because I can see an error, inspect the query log, and work around it. A smart bulb, however, cannot explain that its login endpoint, telemetry host, and command service sit behind related domains. If any of those domains is blocked, it just stops responding. Relaxing your filters for everything will get the device back online, but it weakens security for devices that benefited from the stronger blocklists in the first place.
Your smart home gets its own DNS lane, and the chaos stops
Different devices, different policies, same hardware if you're lazy
My solution was to treat smart-home devices as a class of their own. They already live on an isolated 2.4 GHz network, so I assigned that network a dedicated DNS resolver. A separate physical server is optional here; another Pi-hole or AdGuard Home container, VM, or instance on existing hardware works just as well. The difference is the policy, not the service running it.
The router's DHCP service advertises the IoT resolver only to clients on that specific network, while my trusted network continues using the stricter resolver. Pi-hole can also assign clients to groups with different lists and rules, so the same result is possible with one instance if the resolver can reliably identify each client. AdGuard Home also supports client-specific settings and domain-specific upstream resolvers.
This separation gives you a sane default. Computers and phones keep aggressive ad, malware, and tracking protection while smart home devices get a smaller, security-focused blocklist in addition to explicit blocks for tested telemetry domains that don't break my devices. If a vendor endpoint is required for setup, authentication, notifications, or firmware checks, I allow it only on the IoT policy. I no longer have to punch a network-wide hole to revive one temperamental smart plug.
Query logs finally matter when they're only about your gadgets
Find the one domain your smart plug needs, then stop guessing
The biggest hassle of this approach is that there's no universal blocklist you can download off the internet and use here. The domains you end up blocking will be specific to the smart devices you have around the house, so you're going to have to dig through the logs. The upside is that instead of searching through thousands of queries from browsers, apps, and operating systems, you can see exactly what your smart devices request around the time a feature failed. Then, you can temporarily disable filtering for that client, reproduce the problem, compare the results, and allow only the minimum necessary domain.
That doesn't make every query malicious or prove what data a device sends. DNS reveals the hostnames a device tries to reach, not the contents of an encrypted connection. Still, the smaller dataset makes patterns obvious, such as repeated telemetry lookups, unexpected third-party services, or a device that keeps contacting the cloud even when you control it locally. DNS filtering can be a useful control point, but it complements LAN rules and outbound firewall restrictions instead of simply replacing them.
Names beat numbers: ha.home.arpa instead of 192.168.something
RFC 8375 gave your LAN a suffix, and .local can stay out of it
A side benefit of running a dedicated smart-home resolver is that I also made it authoritative for internal names. This means that instead of typing an IP address and port number every time I wanted to access a service, I can now use URLs like ha.home.arpa for Home Assistant, mqtt.home.arpa for my MQTT broker, and so on. Both Pi-hole and AdGuard Home support local records or DNS rewrites that map a hostname to a LAN address.
I used home.arpa on purpose. RFC 8375 reserves it for non-unique naming inside residential networks and says those queries should be answered locally rather than forwarded onto the internet. This also saved me the hassle of inventing a suffix and didn't overload .local, which belongs to multicast DNS and is supposed to be resolved on the local link using mDNS.
Internal naming also removed hard-coded IP addresses from dashboards, scripts, and Home Assistant integrations. If I move a service to another host, I update one DNS record instead of scanning through configuration files. DNS rewrites can also provide split-horizon behavior, where the same public hostname resolves to a private address at home and its public address elsewhere, a common pattern for Home Assistant setups.
Congratulations, you now run critical infrastructure
Backups, a second resolver, and IoT devices that ignore you anyway
The biggest problem with this approach is the fact that a dedicated resolver quickly becomes infrastructure you have to maintain. It needs a stable address, backups, monitored storage, and preferably a second resolver. Advertising a public resolver as secondary is not a clean failover, as clients may use either server and end up bypassing local filtering or internal names. Both advertised addresses should therefore enforce the same local policy.
Some IoT products also use hard-coded resolvers or encrypted DNS. I ended up handling ordinary external DNS with firewall rules that redirect or block port 53 from the IoT LAN, but encrypted DNS requires more intentional controls and can be difficult to separate from regular HTTPS traffic. IPv6 also needs attention, since an overlooked router advertisement can hand devices a resolver that bypasses the IPv4 setup.
Privacy works better when it isn't one-size-fits-nobody
A looser smart-home policy made the whole network safer, somehow
In the end, the biggest improvement isn't blocking more domains, it was accepting that privacy controls should match the device. My smart home DNS is intentionally less aggressive, yet the overall network is more private because I no longer weaken the main policy whenever an appliance breaks. At the same time, local service names make setup and access easier to move, document, and repair.
DNS won't suddenly make shady devices trustworthy, but it does give you clearer boundaries, a focused log, and a controlled place to decide what each device may resolve. That small architectural change finally allows reliability and privacy to coexist instead of taking turns breaking each other.
articles.summary:
Implementing separate DNS policies for smart home devices and personal computers allows users to maintain aggressive privacy protections while preventing IoT connectivity issues caused by over-blocking.

### Key Points
- Network administrators can use Pi-hole or AdGuard Home to assign distinct DNS filtering policies to specific device groups or isolated 2.4 GHz IoT networks.
- Creating a dedicated IoT DNS lane prevents smart devices from losing connectivity due to blocked telemetry or authentication endpoints required for basic functionality.
- Using local DNS records, such as the RFC 8375-compliant .home.arpa suffix, simplifies internal network management by replacing hard-coded IP addresses with human-readable hostnames.
- Analyzing query logs for a specific device class makes it easier to identify and whitelist necessary domains without compromising the security of the broader network.
- Maintaining a secondary resolver and implementing firewall rules for port 53 ensures consistent policy enforcement and prevents devices from bypassing local DNS settings.

### Why it Matters
Segmenting network traffic by device type balances the need for robust privacy with the operational requirements of cloud-dependent smart home hardware. This architectural approach reduces maintenance overhead by eliminating the need to constantly adjust global blocklists when individual appliances fail.

articles.title: Alphabet’s chief investment officer responds to Jefferies warning that the most likely outcome of the AI boom is massive U.S. capital destruction
articles.author: Alyson Shontell
articles.content:
This essay appears in the Oct. 17, 2026 edition of the Fortune 500 Digest newsletter, which rounds up the headlines driving the week’s most important business news and coverage of Fortune 500 companies. Subscribe to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning.
The AI buildout is in full swing, and it’s incredibly expensive.
Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta, over $720 billion of capital expenditures is projected to be spent this year, most of it on AI infrastructure, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg. Alphabet President and Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat confirmed to me this week at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit that Alphabet intends to spend “significantly more” in 2027. 
This year, Alphabet said it expects capital expenditures of $195 billion to $205 billion. That’s more than double the $91.4 billion it spent in 2025. When asked whether spending on the buildout has peaked across the industry, Porat said it is still in its early phases relative to the eventual economic value Alphabet thinks AI can drive. “We do see this as an opportunity that extends for quite some time,” she said.
Increasingly, debt is fueling the AI buildout too. Private credit funds such as Blue Owl, Apollo, and KKR are a growing source: Outstanding private loans to AI-related companies have climbed to more than $200 billion by some estimates. Often, they’re lending to special purpose vehicles and smaller “neocloud” operators rather than to deep-pocketed Big Tech players. Even Alphabet posted negative free cash flow in Q2 for the first time since its 2004 IPO to help fund AI. Its long-term debt was about $98 billion at the end of June, up more than four times the year prior.
Alphabet can afford such costly long-term AI bets—and arguably the bigger risk for it would be not making them. But many less well-capitalized players are vulnerable, and recent shifts may be making them more so.
One of the biggest: Open-weight models, particularly from China, are increasingly taking business and usage from closed models like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google’s Gemini. New financial figures from Anthropic this week also suggest its growth may have flattened.
This trend led Jefferies’ global head of equity strategy, Chris Wood, to declare that the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom is massive capital destruction in the U.S., according to Bloomberg. Wood argued that cheaper Chinese open-source models threaten to commoditize large language models, eroding the economics behind America’s AI spending, and that China “has become a technological peer to the U.S. in AI.”
When I recently spoke with one of China’s leading open-weight model developers, Moonshot AI, I learned that 70% of its usage comes from outside China.
I asked Porat directly about Wood’s thesis that much of the money pouring into the U.S. AI race could be destroyed.
“It’s illogical to say we’re in a capacity-constrained position because there’s such strong demand for the insight in the ability to improve business and government, and yet you can’t drive a return on it,” Porat replied. She also noted that when it comes to the trend toward open-weight models versus closed, she feels AI companies that add differentiated value will find customers paying for their services regardless.
Porat has had a front-row seat to previous bubbles, first as head of Morgan Stanley’s technology banking team during the dot-com era, and later during the 2008 financial crisis, when she helped advise then U.S. Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson. She went on to become Morgan Stanley’s CFO in 2010.
Her takeaway from those periods is that companies using AI to build truly differentiated experiences will win.
“One of the key lessons from the financial crisis was that you should identify your greatest source of vulnerability early and fortify against it, because you can’t address it in the moment. For banks, it was liquidity. Without liquidity, you couldn’t run a trading operation. Without liquidity, you shut down,” Porat said.
“I’ve been asked that question frequently since: What is the greatest source of vulnerability today? I think for all of us across industry, one of the most important elements is innovation in your business. If anyone is connecting with your customers in ways you are not, because they are using AI and you are not, you’re at a competitive disadvantage.”
Yes, she’s talking her book here, and the “just add more AI” view doesn’t negate the potential systemic economic risk of overbuilding. But it’s also true that AI is not going away and the need for companies to adapt is only going to increase.
At Alphabet, Porat indicated that the company will keep investing heavily in AI because of its conviction in the long-term economic upside.
“You must invest for long term growth,” Porat said. “By the time you need it, it’s too late to say, OK, now we’re going to start.”
For more, check out my full conversation with Google CIO and President Ruth Porat here.
articles.summary:
Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta are projected to spend over $720 billion on AI infrastructure this year, fueling a massive industry-wide capital expenditure surge for long-term growth.

### Key Points
- Alphabet expects 2026 capital expenditures between $195 billion and $205 billion, more than double its 2025 spending.
- Private credit firms like Blue Owl, Apollo, and KKR have provided over $200 billion in loans to support AI-related companies and neocloud operators.
- Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in Q2 2026 for the first time since its 2004 IPO to prioritize AI investment.
- Analysts warn that the rise of cheaper, open-weight models from China could commoditize the AI market and lead to significant capital destruction.
- Alphabet President Ruth Porat maintains that heavy investment is necessary to avoid competitive disadvantages and capture long-term economic value.

### Why it Matters
The massive capital outlay highlights a high-stakes gamble on AI's future profitability despite growing concerns regarding market overcapacity and economic risk. Companies that fail to integrate AI-driven innovation risk long-term obsolescence, forcing firms to balance aggressive infrastructure spending against potential financial instability.

articles.title: MapQuest now shows you Flock and other license plate reader cameras on your route
articles.author: Lauren Edmonds
articles.content:
MapQuest, the OG software to find your way from point A to point B, is taking on the surveillance state.
The free mapping service unveiled a new feature for its mobile app on Thursday that allows users to turn on a "surveillance layer" on a map to locate known automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, along their route.
MapQuest says the app can identify cameras developed by Flock Safety, Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions, and PlateSmart, among others.
"The Roads Have Eyes!" the company said in its BlueSky post announcing the new feature.
MapQuest's General Manager Doug Berger said drivers using the service inspired the company to add the feature.
"We build around what drivers ask for, and showing surveillance camera locations is one of our users' top three requests," Berger told Business Insider in a statement."
License plate readers capture images of vehicles and then use machine learning to turn details such as license plate numbers, car make, color, and model into searchable data. They're commonly found at intersections, parking lots, roadways, highways, and neighborhood entrances, businesses, and private properties.
Law enforcement agencies initially embraced license plate readers to help them locate vehicles and identify suspects. Retail outlets have also used Flock cameras as part of their security efforts.
A major backlash against the cameras, however, has led stores, police, and towns to dial back their use.
Critics say the cameras raise privacy concerns and that the data they collect can be misused or shared with federal immigration officials. Some people who've opposed the cameras have staged protests, launched petitions, and even forcibly removed them.
The city of Tempe in Arizona said in August it shut down its Flock Safety camera network and planned to terminate its contract. Other towns followed suit.
"These cameras have helped our police officers do their jobs, and we don't discount that," Tempe Mayor Corey Woods said in a public statement at the time. "But the risk of misuse is too great. We have to be able to provide public safety in a way that maintains the trust of our community. For Tempe, that means taking these cameras down."
Flock says its license plate readers do not use facial recognition and that customers — meaning the ones putting up the cameras — can control access to and sharing of the data collected. Amid growing backlash, the company has tightened its privacy safeguards, including reducing the time data is retained from 30 days to 7 days.
"They are built to focus on the vehicle involved in an incident and the details that can help distinguish it from other vehicles on the road," Flock told Business Insider in August.
MapQuest first launched in the late 1990s, allowing users to map out a route and print directions. The release of Google Maps eventually obliterated the service. As it tries to stay relevant, it has jumped at opportunities to leverage prevailing public discourse.
In August, MapQuest briefly topped app stores after it — unlike Google — rebuffed President Donald Trump's executive order to rename "Lake Ontario" to "Lake America."
articles.summary:
MapQuest has introduced a new mobile app feature that allows users to identify the locations of automated license plate readers along their planned driving routes for increased privacy.

### Key Points
- The new "surveillance layer" identifies cameras manufactured by companies including Flock Safety, Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions, and PlateSmart.
- Automated license plate readers capture vehicle data such as license plate numbers, make, model, and color using machine learning technology.
- MapQuest added the feature in response to user demand, citing it as one of the top three requests from their driver base.
- Public backlash against surveillance technology has led some municipalities, such as Tempe, Arizona, to terminate contracts with camera providers like Flock Safety.
- Flock Safety has responded to privacy concerns by reducing data retention periods from 30 days to 7 days and clarifying that their systems do not use facial recognition.

### Why it Matters
This feature highlights the growing public tension regarding the widespread use of surveillance technology in public and private spaces. By providing transparency into camera locations, MapQuest is positioning itself as a privacy-conscious alternative in a competitive mapping market.

articles.title: I Test Home Security Tech. Here Are 4 Devices I Rely on to Guard My Porch
articles.author: Tyler Lacoma
articles.content:
Your front door is your first line of defense against, well, anything you don’t want in your home. It’s also one of the first places burglars check when they’re looking for an easy break-in, and the spot porch pirates watch if they think lucrative packages are going to show up. That means your door is also the best place to start improving home security, especially as the holidays ramp up and you get more visitors and deliveries.
Here’s the technology I use to protect my front door and porch, in four easy steps anyone can start with. You don’t need to install a full security system or pay a high monthly subscription for home monitoring with these devices, either. Setup is totally DIY and takes very little time, too. See which you should start with.
A smart lock to control access from anywhere
Old deadbolts do well, but any entryway can get a powerful upgrade by adding digital features via a smart lock. Smart locks allow you to control your front door lock from anywhere using your phone, as well as creating temporary passes for guests. They can support digital wallet keys for touchless unlocking, and many have keypads or fingerprint readers. Plus, you can enable settings like auto-locking, so you never have to worry about forgetting to lock the door.
More from CNET
Smart locks come in two flavors: retrofits that leave your deadbolt largely intact and only replace your indoor thumb turn, and full deadbolt replacements that give you new locking power, inside and out. Don’t worry about installation: If you’ve never installed a deadbolt before, the process is generally easy and doesn’t take much time. I have a full guide where you can find more details.
What models do you recommend?
A video doorbell for smart alerts about what’s happening
Say goodbye to dusty doorbells of the past. Today’s high-tech doorbells do far more than chime: Video doorbells keep an eye on your front porch, while also giving you a two-way audio intercom right on your phone to hold a conversation — or even let an LLM do the talking for you.
Video doorbells also have particularly useful object recognition features, sometimes even for free. That includes recognizing packages and alerting you whenever one shows up at your door, or when one suddenly vanishes. Video storage options can save recordings of key events, so you can check who came to the door if you need to.
These advanced doorbells come in both wired and wireless versions. I’m a fan of the battery-powered, wireless models, which you can set and angle to get just the right look at your porch, doormat and other key places. Many can also work with your current door chime, although you probably don’t need it anymore with phone-based chimes.
What models do you recommend?
- Google Nest’s compact, universal battery model ($180)
- Tapo’s 4K beast with local video storage ($220)
- Blink’s ultra-affordable doorbell ($80)
A delivery box to protect packages
Package theft concerns have reignited a centuries-old tradition of protecting mail. Today’s modern delivery boxes are specifically designed to allow delivery people to put packages inside, but make it difficult or impossible for thieves to take packages out, through clever lock models, auto-locking, smart controls and other various tricks.
I’ve been using a delivery box myself for a couple of years and find it very handy, as long as you have the space by your door. Some versions even come weighted or screwed down if you’re worried about a porch pirate absconding with the entire box. It’s a good idea to put notes in your deliveries to use the box, since despite signs not all delivery people will notice it’s there.
As a final plus, these boxes also keep your packages protected from the elements, which is nice when you live in an area that gets frequent winter snowstorms, as I do.
What models do you recommend?
A smart bulb for powerful lighting
Where front doors exist, there’s usually a light nearby, like an overhead porch light or a wall-mounted lamp, to illuminate the entryway and surrounding area. These lights can also get a major makeover if you switch to an LED smart bulb, which are available as both BR30 floodlights and standard A19 home bulbs.
These lights also give you phone app controls, which is more important than it might seem. With my apps, I can control brightness, set schedules for bulbs to turn on or off, and even adjust the color to whatever I want, say for a holiday event. All it takes is screwing in the bulb and connecting it to Wi-Fi, so you can be done in seconds.
If you feel like experimenting, you can usually link smart bulbs to other devices, too. For example, you could set the light to turn on automatically when a smart lock is unlocked, or when a security system is disarmed.
What models do you recommend?
- GE Cync’s four-quadrant Dynamic Effect floodlight bulb ($21)
- Wiz’s highly affordable standard-sized bulb 2-pack ($22)
- Ecosmart’s durable, extra-large floodlight bulb 2-pack ($14)
Now that your front porch is up to date, take a look at the latest home AI tricks I’ve found are actually worth using and how to get them.
articles.summary:
Homeowners can significantly improve front door security and deter package theft by installing DIY-friendly smart locks, video doorbells, secure delivery boxes, and automated smart lighting systems.

### Key Points
- Smart locks enable remote access control, temporary guest passes, and auto-locking features to replace or augment traditional deadbolts.
- Video doorbells provide two-way audio and object recognition to alert users about package deliveries or suspicious activity on the porch.
- Secure delivery boxes protect parcels from both theft and weather conditions using specialized locking mechanisms and weighted designs.
- Smart LED bulbs allow for remote brightness, color, and schedule adjustments, which can be linked to other security devices for automated lighting.
- Recommended hardware includes Google Nest, Tapo, and Blink doorbells, alongside GE Cync and Wiz smart lighting solutions.

### Why it Matters
Upgrading entryways with these connected devices provides a cost-effective, DIY alternative to expensive, subscription-based home security systems. These tools offer homeowners greater peace of mind and practical protection against porch piracy and unauthorized access during the busy holiday season.

articles.title: Personal Data for Millions of California Students Stolen in Massive Breach
articles.author: EditorDavid
articles.content:
Millions of current and former students at California's public school have had their data stolen — including names, date of birth, and addresses — stolen in a breach, reports the Los Angeles Times.
The breach affects students "who took the state's mandated standardized tests that annually assess their academic proficiency, education officials announced Friday."
The compromised information affects many more than the state's current 5.7 million public-school students as the breach dates back to 2023 enrollments. Students who left California but did not confirm their transfer to another school also were affected, dating back to 2006. 
The data breach involved [nonprofit] Educational Testing Service or ETS, which provides extensive services to California [including test participation and assessment data]... Affected former students, including those who are now adults, are eligible for 24 months of free identity-protection services and identity-restoration help if there is identity theft.  Officials said that parents and guardians may want to consider requesting a free credit freeze for their children who are under 16 to help prevent unauthorized accounts from being opened in the names of their children.
 
The breach involved a compromised login credential, according to a web page about the incident from California's Department of Education. The compromised credential was then used to copy files with student information at "various" times between May 22 and September 18, 2026, which drew concern from a cybersecurity expert interviewed by the Los Angeles Times:
"A stolen login credential should not become a months-long passport to millions of students' personal records," said Anton Dahbura, executive director of the Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute. "If that is what happened here, the critical question is why authentication safeguards, access restrictions, and monitoring systems failed to detect and stop the unauthorized activity."
He added: "Incidents like this expose a fundamental weakness in how we manage student data: School systems may outsource the storage and processing of sensitive information, but they cannot outsource the consequences of a breach. When millions of student records are concentrated with a single vendor, one security failure can become a statewide problem with consequences that follow children for years."
  
A spokesperson for ETS told the Times that they've now implemented additional safeguards, including strengthened access controls, enhanced monitoring, and more third-party review of their security practices.
articles.summary:
Millions of current and former California public school students have had their personal data compromised following a significant security breach at the Educational Testing Service.

### Key Points
- The breach exposed sensitive information including names, dates of birth, and addresses for students who took state-mandated standardized tests.
- Compromised records date back to 2006, affecting both current students and those who have since left the California public school system.
- Unauthorized access occurred between May 22 and September 18, 2026, via a single compromised login credential used to copy files.
- Educational Testing Service (ETS) has implemented strengthened access controls and enhanced monitoring to prevent future unauthorized data access.
- Affected individuals are eligible for 24 months of free identity-protection services and identity-restoration assistance.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the systemic risks associated with outsourcing sensitive student data to third-party vendors that manage large-scale information repositories. The breach underscores the critical need for robust authentication and monitoring safeguards to prevent single points of failure from impacting millions of individuals.

articles.title: Rank Tracker Data, ChatGPT Tags & AI Search Links – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.author: Matt G. Southern
articles.content:
Welcome to the Pulse: This week, we’re looking at how much you can rely on your rankings and ChatGPT referral numbers, how Google and Bing display links and citations in AI search, and what Google is hiring for in Discover.
Here’s what matters for you and your work.
Some Tracked Google Results Lost Most Of Their Usual Sites
From Sept. 13 to Oct. 9, 8.0% of the Google results pages that rank-tracking company Nozzle could check against each keyword’s history were missing most of the keyword’s usual sites, which then came back on a later check, according to the company’s analysis. Nozzle collected those 17.8 million pages through automated searches.
Key facts:
That compares with 0.17% from Aug. 20 to Sept. 9. The share peaked at about a quarter of pages from Sept. 27 to 29 and has run at about 5% to 11% a day since Oct. 1. Nozzle describes these pages as “poisoned” and attributes the pattern to Google’s response to AI scraping. The report also doesn’t include a statement from Google. For keywords where a customer’s own site would typically rank, that site didn’t appear in the top 10 on 58.6% of affected pages, compared with 2.7% in the baseline.
Why This Matters
Before adding a one-day drop from late September or October to a client report, compare the keyword with the sites that usually ranked on page 1 before mid-September (the baseline Nozzle uses). If Search Console shows a similar drop in impressions and clicks for the same query and page, the decline is more likely to be real.
Read our full coverage: Analysis: Google Is Poisoning Search Results For Rank Trackers
ChatGPT Referral Drop Tied To Links Missing Their Tracking Tag
ChatGPT-attributed sessions in Google Analytics 4 fell sharply this month. Analysts link the drop to inline links in ChatGPT’s answers that stopped carrying the utm_source=chatgpt.com tag after GPT-6 rolled out.
Key facts:
Graphite CEO Ethan Smith wrote on LinkedIn that there was an approximate 45% drop in ChatGPT sessions on sites tracked by Graphite with meaningful AI Assistant Channel traffic in GA4, and that the untagged visit data could appear under the “Direct” label. Adobe’s Cedric Huesler added that OpenAI confirmed a known bug to him on October 14, and that they had started deploying a fix for this issue on October 15. At around 9 a.m. PT on October 15, according to Huesler, tagged ChatGPT clicks returned to roughly 95-100% of the same hour from the previous week across thousands of websites that he has been tracking. In contrast, SEO consultant Glenn Gabe replied that he hadn’t seen the change yet; and although OpenAI’s release notes were updated on October 15, they did not reference the above-mentioned bug or solution.
Why This Matters
Huesler places the affected window between Oct. 8 and 15. He and Smith recommend noting it in your reports so no one mistakes the dip for lost traffic. Since most ChatGPT clicks still arrive without a referrer, Huesler suggests tracking them by their UTM tag.
Read our full coverage: ChatGPT Traffic Drop Appears To Be A Tracking Problem
Google Is Moving Inline Links Higher In More AI Responses
Google is changing how links appear in AI Mode and AI Overviews, including updates that show inline links higher in responses more often.
Key facts:
Google also plans to test a section at the top of some responses that links to official pages for specific tasks. It’s starting to roll out its carousels for timely articles, which highlight a user’s Preferred Sources, to more locations and languages, though the post doesn’t name them. This week, Google also started testing creator and publisher names on AI Mode video results that link to Search profiles.
Why This Matters
In Search Console, each link in an AI Overview is given the same position as that of the overall AI overview. Therefore, moving an inline link higher doesn’t by itself change its reported position. Users who have designated you as a preferred source can see your site highlighted in more carousels as they expand. Your website has to be included in Search generative AI features in Search Console for you to even qualify as a preferred source, as documented on Google’s documentation website.
Read our full coverage: Google Puts Inline Links Higher In More AI Search Responses
Bing’s AI Performance Report Adds Topics And Opportunity Queries
Microsoft added a beta feature called Topics Portfolio to the AI Performance report in Bing Webmaster Tools.
Key facts:
It groups the queries your site is cited for in AI answers into broader topics, with approximate figures for each topic’s total citations across all sites, the number of sites cited, and the number of queries. It also lists opportunity queries, where other sites appear and yours doesn’t, with citation volumes shown as ranges. The view only appears if Bing has enough data for your site.
Why This Matters
The opportunity query list from Bing is a way for content teams to identify potential gaps in coverage of topics on their sites. However, this can also contain competitor brand terms which may be irrelevant to your website. Microsoft says to treat Topics Portfolio’s metrics as directional rather than absolute, which makes them better for comparing different topics but less useful if you need to track an exact count.
Read our full coverage: Bing Webmaster Tools Sorts AI Search Queries Into Topics
Google Discover Job Listings Describe AI-Generated Content
Open Google job listings describe teams that generate and recommend AI content for Discover.
Key facts:
A Staff ML Engineer listing says the Discover Feed Recommendation team “leads by recommending AI-generated content (AIGC) to fulfill user interests.” It also describes agentic flows that generate content for what the listing calls proactive surfaces, naming Discover and Notifications. A director-level design listing describes turning Discover into a “proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience,” working with teams at YouTube, Shopping, Chrome, and Android.
Why This Matters
Neither Discover listing gives a timeline or says how much of the feed AI content would fill. Search Console’s generative AI report for Discover is where your data shows Discover’s AI features linking to your site, with impressions as the only metric its help page describes.
Read our full coverage: Google Is Hiring To Generate AI Content For Discover and Google Discover To Undergo Dramatic Changes
Theme Of The Week: A Cross-Check For Every Number
Rank-tracker and ChatGPT referral numbers changed this week. The changes were based on how the numbers were gathered. articles.title: Pirate Chain Exploit Creates 39.8 Million Unauthorized Tokens In Major Security Breach
articles.author: Bitcoinist Editorial Team
articles.content:
TL;DR: Pirate Chain developers disclosed a vulnerability linked to roughly 39.8 million unauthorized ARRR tokens. The incident raised urgent questions about network supply and how an attack can be investigated when transactions use strong privacy protections.
Privacy-focused cryptocurrency Pirate Chain faced a major security crisis after developers reported that unauthorized tokens had been created through a validation flaw.
The incident, discussed publicly in mid-October, involved approximately 39.8 million ARRR. That amount was substantial relative to the currency’s existing supply.
The project’s privacy features made it difficult to follow the affected funds once they entered shielded transaction pools.
The Problem Was Not A Broken Encryption Algorithm
Developers attributed the issue to implementation and validation errors rather than demonstrating that the underlying zero-knowledge cryptography had been defeated.
That distinction is important. A blockchain can use sophisticated privacy technology and still contain flaws in the rules determining which transactions are accepted.
Exchanges and network participants responded with precautionary restrictions while the team investigated.
Because shielded funds do not reveal the same public transaction information as ordinary transparent blockchain transfers, outsiders cannot easily determine every movement involving the unauthorized tokens.
Restoring Trust Will Be Difficult
A normal software patch can prevent a flaw from being exploited again, but it does not automatically settle questions about tokens already created.
The project must consider the impact on legitimate holders, exchange trading and the integrity of its recorded supply.
Recovery measures can also be controversial in decentralised networks, especially if they involve changing how previously confirmed activity is treated.
For Pirate Chain, the immediate task is technical repair. The longer-term challenge is persuading investors that the network can provide dependable monetary rules alongside transaction privacy.
Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

Pirate Chain developers have identified a critical validation flaw that allowed for the unauthorized creation of approximately 39.8 million ARRR tokens, raising significant concerns regarding network supply integrity.

### Key Points
- Developers discovered a vulnerability that enabled the unauthorized minting of 39.8 million ARRR tokens.
- The flaw stemmed from implementation and validation errors rather than a failure of the underlying zero-knowledge encryption.
- Privacy-focused shielded transaction pools have complicated efforts to track the movement of the illicitly created assets.
- Exchanges and network participants implemented precautionary restrictions following the mid-October disclosure of the security incident.
- The project team is currently evaluating recovery measures to address the impact on the total circulating supply.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the inherent difficulty of auditing and remediating security breaches within privacy-centric blockchain networks where transaction data remains obscured. The challenge of restoring investor confidence underscores the tension between maintaining absolute user anonymity and ensuring the long-term stability of a digital currency's monetary policy.

articles.title: ServiceNow AI Control Tower: Selling a penthouse while building the frame
articles.author: Dave Vellante
articles.content:
ServiceNow AI Control Tower: Selling a penthouse while building the frame
ServiceNow Inc. is making one of the more consequential and visible bets in enterprise artificial intelligence. The company says AI Control Tower can discover and govern any agent, work across models and clouds, track cost and value, and shut down behavior that violates policy.
That sales pitch plays directly to ServiceNow’s greatest asset – its installed base. Information technology and service management or ITSM, configuration management database or CMDB, risk workflows, security operations and years of operating context give the company a distribution and data advantage most AI and governance vendors do not have.
Our research suggests that moat is real. But proprietary customer data shows a more nuanced picture. Control Tower is already strong as a governance workflow and system of action. It can inventory AI assets, connect risks to owners, route approvals and remediation, and preserve an audit trail. What the field study has not broadly validated is the claim that Control Tower is a complete technical governance and runtime enforcement plane across the heterogeneous enterprise.
In this Breaking Analysis episode, we use a methodology similar to our CoreWeave analysis, and pressure-test management’s statements against 15 in-depth interviews with ServiceNow customers conducted with our data partner, Qualitate. We ask the following question: Is Control Tower becoming the enterprise AI control plane – or is it limited to the governance system of action?
Three distinct technical jobs – ServiceNow dominates only one today
ServiceNow may not need to own every technical control to build a very large business bolstered by AI governance. It can create enormous value by owning the workflow around those controls – inventory, accountability, approvals, exceptions, remediation and audit history.
But its marketing pitch is allowing customers to think the the market is collapsing three jobs into one convenient phrase: AI governance.
The first is governance workflow and accountability. This is where ServiceNow is strongest.
The second is AI lifecycle evidence – model versions, lineage, validation, bias, explainability and drift. ServiceNow can coordinate that evidence, but customers often generate it elsewhere.
The third is runtime enforcement and AI security – intercepting an action, blocking a deployment, constraining an agent or revoking access in real time. Our survey indicates this layer is frequently external, custom or human.
The nuance is that approving a model and assigning a remediation ticket are valuable. But they are not the same as technically validating the model, proving lineage or blocking the action.
ServiceNow’s opportunity is to connect all three. It is not best-of-breed in each today according to its own customers. Broadly, buyers should be cautious of claims that ServiceNow AI Control Tower is a platform that is universally end-to-end.
The five pillars of ServiceNow’s AI strategy
Control Tower sits inside a broader ServiceNow agentic AI strategy built on five connected pillars as shown below.
First is a model-agnostic posture: Any model, agent, cloud, data source or system of record.
Second is the shift from chat assistants to autonomous workers that plan, execute and adapt across workflows.
Third is centralized governance through AI Control Tower – discovery, ownership, access, observability, value and remediation.
Fourth is AI cost and value management: Token economics, model selection, budget control and ROI.
Fifth is pricing and packaging. Foundation, Advanced and Prime tiers seed AI broadly, move customers up the stack and add consumption on top of subscriptions.
These pillars reinforce one another and describe ServiceNow’s advantage and momentum. More agents create more governance demand. Model choice creates complexity. Governance addresses complexity and creates more reasons to stay on the platform. And more usage drives more consumption.
Our focus today is the key link in that flywheel chain: Can AI Control Tower can extend ServiceNow’s workflow advantage into technical governance and runtime control?
The numbers underscore ServiceNow’s AI momentum
Management’s “right-to-win” argument is not that ServiceNow builds the best foundation models. It is that ServiceNow already knows how work moves through the enterprise.
Bill McDermott describes the moat in one word: context.
ServiceNow says its platform supports roughly 100 billion workflows and nearly 8 trillion transactions. Amit Zavery said more than 500 customers were live with AI Control Tower in the first six months. And ServiceNow reported AI ACV above 1 billion dollars in Q2, with a full-year target of $1.5 billion.
The CMDB knows assets, services, owners and dependencies. ITSM and change management know how work is routed and approved. IRM understands controls, risks, issues and evidence.
A best-of-breed specialist will likely have deeper model analytics, but it often lacks the operational graph that identifies the owner, business service or the path to remediate an issue.
The installed base gives ServiceNow a right to compete. It does not, by itself, prove that every technical control is present or every runtime path is governed.
Field study of 15 ServiceNow customers
A quick word on methodology.
TheCUBE Research commissioned a study through its partner, Qualitate, which conducted the fieldwork from Sept. 15-21, 2026.
The final base is 15 completed large-enterprise interviews totaling 575 minutes. Eleven respondents were in North America and four in Europe. Five came from financial services, four from healthcare, three from technology and telecommunications, and three from public sector, manufacturing or other industries.
The sample was senior: three executives or vice presidents, 10 directors or functional heads, and two senior managers.
Every respondent had an existing ServiceNow footprint. The study is a deliberate qualitative study of expansion, coexistence, implementation and control boundaries inside real accounts. Eleven of the 15 customers had either installed, piloted or were actively evaluating ServiceNow AI Control Tower.
There’s of course a bias toward the ServiceNow installed base. That is by design and it’s useful because management’s premise is it has an installed-base premise. We are testing the environment where Control Tower should have its greatest advantage.
Our methodology specifically separates direct experience from management claims. This is not a survey with 15 customers supplied by ServiceNow.
ServiceNow is building on its workflow and operational moat
This next chart speaks to the heart of the episode.
All 15 respondents recognized ServiceNow’s workflow, operational integration or incumbency advantage.
Fourteen of 15, however described runtime enforcement as external, custom, human mediated, limited to selected paths or not proven at enterprise scale. The one exception was a limited financial-services pilot that successfully tested ServiceNow’s blocking capability for at least one model and one agent.
Twelve of 15 identified a model-specific evidence gap – validation records, lineage, bias, explainability, drift history or AI-specific regulatory artifacts.
And twelve of 15 tied governance value or switching cost to the wider Now Platform – mainly ITSM, CMDB, change management and SecOps.
Our research shows that the same ServiceNow architecture creates both the moat and the boundary limits. Specifically, ServiceNow is hard to displace because governance work is embedded in operations. But the value story degrades when the CMDB is immature, the AI estate sits outside ServiceNow control paths, or regulators require technical evidence generated elsewhere.
One respondent called ServiceNow more like a governance orchestration layer than the actual governance of AI. We would challenge that a bit: It is real governance, but strongest at orchestrating accountability and action.
Regarding CMDB – when we first started covering ServiceNow in 2013, ServiceNow management would constantly push customers to consolidate on a single CMDB, which today is the norm. This has given ServiceNow a tremendous incumbency advantage but customers encounter friction.
A senior engineering manager at a large North American financial services company summed it up like this:
The CMDB dependency is bigtime on this because it must be cleaned up quite often, and that is the reason there are a lot of surveys that have been sent within the organization to actually clean up the CMDB on a regular basis. And a lot of auditing around is to be done as part of that.
Unpacking the three fundamental operating layers of AI governance
The interviews suggest that AI governance is separating into three operating layers, with different buyers and budgets as shown below.
The first is governance workflow and accountability: Here we mean inventory, ownership, approvals, exceptions, issues, remediation and audit history. ServiceNow has the clearest advantage here.
The second is AI lifecycle evidence and regulatory proof: We’re talking about functions like model versions, lineage, validation, bias, explainability, drift and performance history. Hyperscaler-native tools, model platforms and specialists often supply this layer. Players here include IBM with Watsonx.governance, Fiddler AI; or a company like Credo AI which is strong at regulatory mapping and audit trail.
The third is runtime enforcement and AI security: Gateway policies, permission checks, agent identity, deployment gates and the ability to block or constrain actions. Security and AI platform budgets usually fund it. Palo Alto Prisma AIRS and Cisco AI Defense are good examples here.
This explains why architectures remain multi-vendor even when vendors claim end-to-end governance. There are three different activities involved including:
- The completion of a workflow;
- A model validation artifact – for example, a report generated while evaluating a model to prove how well it works; and
- A blocked action at runtime – versus an asynchronous alert to a human.
The question for ServiceNow is can it own every layer? Or will it become the policy authority and hub for evidence that connects these three layers and acts as the system of action?
This is where the field study we did with Qualitate strongly validates management’s story and at the same time highlights some notable weaknesses.
ServiceNow’s differentiation: Turning a governance finding into actual work
An AI asset can be connected to an application, business service, owner and dependency in the CMDB. IRM can attach controls, risks, issues, evidence and exceptions. ITSM, change management and Action Fabric can route the finding, track remediation and preserve the audit history.
Note: Action Fabric is ServiceNow’s interoperability and governance framework that lets external AI agents like Claude execute multistep workflows inside ServiceNow in a headless manner — similar to the way we reported on Salesforce’s Headless 360 – bypassing the traditional interface.
One respondent put it like this: Day one ServiceNow, day one workflow. Another said the CMDB matters because an AI risk can be connected to the application and business-service owner.
That is important because model-risk tool may detect drift or bias, but if the organization cannot assign, prioritize, remediate and prove what happened, the control has limited operational value.
This is why “just ticketing” is the wrong criticism. Operational accountability is part of governance.
The more accurate description in our view is that ServiceNow is exceptionally well-positioned to be the system of action for AI governance. The question is how much technical evidence and enforcement it can bring into that system.
What an end-to-end architecture should deliver
This next diagram shows what actually flows when the architecture works as advertised.
AI Control Tower discovers the asset and establishes ownership. The CMDB supplies application, service and dependency context. IRM brings policy, risk, control, evidence and exception records. ITSM and Action Fabric turn the finding into assigned remediation work.
That internal path is ServiceNow’s sweet spot.
The limits show up when the organization needs technical model evidence or a live intervention at runtime. The technical validation may come from a model platform or specialist vendor. Blocking may occur in an application programming interface gateway or security product. The telemetry then has to return to Control Tower as evidence.
In several of our customer interviews, that connection was incomplete or fuzzy. Different teams owned governance, model tooling and security. Data models and workflows did not align automatically.
ServiceNow does not have to be the box that blocks every action. But it should define policy, identify the owner, send the decision to the right enforcement point, receive telemetry and preserve the audit trail.
That’s the closed loop.
Caveat emptor of ‘kill switch’ claims
Bill McDermott stated on CNBC’s “Mad Money” in July 2026, that ServiceNow possesses a kill switch to halt rogue AI agents and prevent disruptions, contrasting it with incidents like OpenAI’s agent escaping a test environment and hacking Hugging Face.
Buyer beware on this claim. Our survey exposes the limitations of this assertion.
Only one respondent reported a very positive pilot and that was limited. In this case, at least one model and one agent were tested for blocking, auditors were satisfied, and the respondent gave high marks. So that case directly supports management’s claim in a selected environment.
But the other 14 respondents described runtime control as external, custom, human mediated, limited to selected paths or not proven at scale.
What has not been validated – and appears to be a gap – is universal coverage across Azure OpenAI, custom agents, SaaS copilots, third-party models, shadow AI, multiple clouds and non-ServiceNow workflows.
One security practitioner estimated that only 30% to 40% of total AI activity could realistically pass through ServiceNow control paths today.
Our assessment is the kill-switch claim is overstated. It is not yet proven as a universal enterprise runtime control plane.
Unpacking procedural vs. technical evidence
ServiceNow is strong at procedural proof – showing who approved a use case, which control was completed, who owns the exception, whether remediation occurred and what the audit history looks like. Several respondents said auditors accepted the ServiceNow record.
The gaps become more obvious in high-risk or regulated use cases. Survey respondents indicated ServiceNow gaps in many areas related to what we’re calling technical proof, including: Validation methodology, test dataset, model versions, training-data lineage, bias and fairness results, explainability, drift and performance history, prompt and response evaluations, hallucination and toxicity tests, permission evidence and a record of what the agent did at runtime.
Those artifacts are most often generated by alternative platforms – for example. IBM, hyperscaler-native governance tooling, other model platforms, MLOps systems, privacy and AI governance specialists, or traditional model-risk tools.
Control Tower can still become the place where that evidence is captured, evaluated, linked to policy and operationalized. But ServiceNow is currently out over its skis in our view, using “end-to-end” language. Our survey data suggests that, today anyway, ServiceNow is weaker at showing the complete evidence path for a real model or agent across a heterogeneous environment.
Buying decisions are heavily influenced by ServiceNow footprint and risk
Buying indicators become clearer when we assess two variables: ServiceNow footprint depth and the intensity of AI or model risk. The four quadrants below explain this dynamic in simple terms.
Where ServiceNow is deeply embedded and regulation is modest, Control Tower has its best expansion opportunity – the lower right on this chart. This is the consolidation sweet spot for ServiceNow and probably represents the largest total available market.
The upper right shows where regulation is high and ServiceNow is deep, customers often preserve ServiceNow as the system of action but add independent lifecycle evidence and runtime controls. Coexistence is likely. That’s also a fairly large chunk of the market.
Where regulation is high and the ServiceNow footprint is shallow, the field is open to independent AI governance and model-risk tools. That is shown on the upper left.
Where both are limited, hyperscaler-native controls or lighter specialists may be good enough – lower left.
Our analysis also exposes three different buyer-personas.
- IT operations and platform owners value workflow, context and consolidation;
- Model risk and AI governance teams value technical proof;
- Security teams own runtime control.
The vendor that speaks to only one persona may win the feature argument and still lose the account.
A new pricing and packaging model for AI
ServiceNow’s commercial strategy is worth exploring. This spring, ahead of ServiceNow Knowledge, the company replaced its legacy package tiers (Standard, Professional, Enterprise, Pro Plus and Enterprise Plus) with three AI-native pricing and packaging tiers: Foundation, Advanced and Prime.
Foundation, Advanced and Prime give customers an upgrade path, but some customers bristle. Management reports price uplifts of roughly 20% to 30% in the lower AI tiers and more than 30% in Prime, with subscription commitments paired with usage-based meters.
Our survey supports the momentum in ServiceNow ACVs. It shows that the operating model drives higher invoices. But the data also exposes some meaningful customer friction.
Twelve of 15 respondents said pricing, packaging or total-cost were acute concerns. Thirteen described significant configuration, integration or staffing friction.
As shown above, eight respondents supplied actual data comparing expectations to actual costs. Seven of the eight said costs came in above expectations, and one described the rollout as broadly on budget.
The cost overruns were not from licensing issues alone. They included partners, data normalization, CMDB hygiene, custom workflows, integration engineering, permanent specialists, administration and external controls.
One respondent said: We expected to need ServiceNow specialists, but we underestimated how permanent that would be.
Some verbatim quotes from the customers regarding pricing:
“ServiceNow is expensive”
“the packaging is frustrating”
“We expect costs to increase”
“the proposed quote is too high”
“Our costs came in 30% above our original expectation”
Importantly, this does not mean the value is poor. Some customers justified the extra cost. The issue is predictability. Customers should force ServiceNow to sell a bounded outcome, make integration assumptions explicit and show the full operating cost.
The market is showing distinct budget opportunities
The broader market is fragmenting into different budget layers as shown below. Control Tower touches them all but ServiceNow faces credible competition in each.
Runtime enforcement and AI security include Palo Alto Networks, Guardrails AI, Kong, Lakera, HiddenLayer and Protect AI.
Hyperscaler-native governance includes Microsoft Purview and Azure AI, Bedrock Guardrails and Vertex AI governance.
Specialist or AI governance leaders include IBM, OneTrust, Credo AI, Holistic AI and ModelOp. Traditional GRC and model-risk tools include Archer, AuditBoard, MetricStream, LogicGate and Navex.
Notably, 12 of fifteen respondents were evaluating or deploying separate runtime controls, usually from cybersecurity or AI platform budgets.
The obvious opportunity for ServiceNow is to orchestrate and preserve evidence across all these tools. The risk is that the vendor owning the enforcement point also captures the telemetry, the security buyer and eventually the policy decision. ServiceNow could receive a ticket after the fact instead of controlling the loop.
The answer is potentially openness with authority: Customers choose any enforcement technology while Control Tower remains the policy system, accountability layer and durable evidence system of record to support the overall system of action.
Pressure testing ServiceNow management’s claims
This scorecard below summarizes our test.
The incumbency and context moat is most definitely supported by our survey. All fifteen respondents recognized ServiceNow’s workflow, operational or installed-base advantage.
Model-agnostic orchestration is directionally supported. Customers value broad connectivity, but connector breadth is not the same as control depth.
The end-to-end governance claim is a stretch in our view. Control Tower is strong on inventory, accountability and procedural evidence but model-specific artifacts are frequently generated elsewhere.
The kill-switch claim is also overstated in our view. It is supported for selected pathways but definitely not yet as a universal runtime control plane. One positive pilot is good, but 14 respondents describing external, custom or limited enforcement suggest immaturity.
Execution watch: Cost transparency is an issue. Value management is a credible promise. The packaging creates attach and consumption opportunity but implementation remains a source of friction.
The field is most definitely not saying Control Tower is vaporware. Claims that it’s just a bolt-on are overstated; but its scope is currently limited.
The bottom line is ServiceNow is strongest where governance turns into actual work. It is less proven where governance becomes mathematical model evidence or a real-time intervention across a heterogeneous estate.
The investor angle points to a strong bull case with gaps to fill
From an investor and strategic perspective, the bull case is compelling.
AI Control Tower creates a new attach point into a sticky and powerful installed base. It converts CMDB context into a governance system of action. The model-agnostic posture gives optionality across labs and hyperscalers. And the commercial model creates subscription uplift plus consumption.
But there are areas of concern that we describe below.
Based on our customer surveys, runtime claims are ahead of broad field validation. Model-specific evidence still depends on adjacent tools with better depth. Implementation friction can slow adoption and create cost overrun surprises. Security vendors, deep governance experts and hyperscalers can capture control points and budget.
We believe the business can be excellent without ServiceNow owning every technical control. Orchestration is the strongest position because buyers rarely want to replace every model platform, security product or cloud control. They want a common policy, accountability and action layer.
The company’s valuation has fluctuated substantially peaking in late 2024 at around $230 billion dipping to the mid-$80 billion range in April of this year. It’s market cap is now on the rise again at around $146 billion as of this writing. The market cap debate will rest on how successfully ServiceNow can convince investors that it’s an AI winner; which in part, will depend on the company’s ability to monetize the closed loop we described earlier.
If Control Tower becomes the policy authority and evidence hub, the moat expands. If it only receives alerts after other products make the important decisions, the strategic value is more limited. Our bet is on the former because of the company’s footprint.
Customer action item: Make the closed loop prove itself before you scale
The research does not say Control Tower lacks value. Quite the opposite. Customers consistently value ServiceNow’s workflow, CMDB context, accountability and ability to turn a governance finding into work. But orchestration is not the same thing as technical enforcement, and that distinction is where buyers can get into trouble. In fourteen of the fifteen interviews, broad runtime enforcement was external, custom, human-mediated, limited to selected pathways or not yet proven at enterprise scale.
Start by mapping the control sequence. For one specific model or agent, name the policy owner, the source of model-level evidence, the exact enforcement point, the telemetry path and the remediation owner. Do not accept an architecture in which every arrow disappears into a black box control plane.
Next, test a real violation. Pick a high-risk use case – for example an agent that can access sensitive data, move money, change infrastructure or interact with customers. Trigger a policy breach and show where the action is blocked or constrained. Then verify that the event comes back into the governance record, creates the right case, assigns an owner and preserves the evidence an auditor would need and accept.
Third, price the full operating model – not just the Control Tower license. Include IRM and CMDB dependencies, data normalization, connectors, implementation partners, external runtime controls, AI uplifts, service fees and the recurring specialists needed to maintain the system. Our interviews show that those operating costs are where many programs moved significantly beyond their original expectations.
Finally, protect optionality. This is fundamental to your AI sovereignty. Architect around open APIs, explicit integration responsibilities, service levels and have compensating controls for an exit path. Buyers should have a shared accountability model with their vendors and internal stakeholders. Understand who owns the policy, who owns the enforcement point and who is accountable when a handoff fails.
The buyer gate should be no production-scale growth until one real violation is detected, blocked, recorded and remediated end to end. ServiceNow can be the system of action without being the only control. The buyer’s job is to prove that the entire system works as a system.

articles.title: Nevermind the RAM crisis, these are the 5 things you can do for the best PC gaming experience without overpaying for parts
articles.author: alekshamcloughlin@outlook.com (Aleksha McLoughlin) , Aleksha McLoughlin
articles.content:
I'm not going to sugarcoat it: 2026 has been a terrible time to be a PC gamer. As someone who's been covering computing tech for over a decade and building machines for longer than that, the future looks bleak.
The biggest tech companies in the world are buying up vital components such as RAM and graphics cards to build data centers. Prices for these parts are soaring as demand drastically outpaces supply. Many expect things won't stabilize until at least 2030, so what can we do to get through the worst of it?
While the best graphics cards, NVMe SSDs, and the best DDR5 RAM modules have become expensive and elusive, that's not the case across the board for other computing components, as there are plenty of other essential upgrades you can make to weather the storm and ensure you've got one of the best gaming PCs ready for the flagship releases of the future... provided you keep your expectations in check.
I'm going through the five biggest ways you can maximize your PC gaming experience through this dark and uncertain time. My best advice without spending any additional money is to hold onto what you've got and be smart with your graphics settings and target resolution.
Today's best PC games are optimized with console parity in mind, meaning they have to be able to run on the Xbox Series X/S and PS5, so as long as your GPU is from 2020/2021 or later, you should be okay. If you're looking to spend a little money, though, here's what I recommend doing next.
1. Replace your keyboard and mouse
The average PC gamer replaces their peripherals, such as keyboards, mice, and headsets, every four to five years. If you're reading this at your desk, there's a high chance you're typing on an old deck or scrolling with a past-their-prime pointer.
While this year has been pretty terrible for internal computing components, it's actually been an exciting time of innovation for mice and keyboards, making now the perfect time to take the cash that would have gone on a GPU and to pump life into your setup instead.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I'm a tech journalist, but I'm also an avid esports gamer. 2026 alone has seen some truly stand-out peripherals that have been head and shoulders above what we've had since the RAM crisis began. My top recommendations right now include the excellent Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike with its second-generation HITS tech, or you can stick to tried-and-true analog with the stellar Razer Viper V4 Pro, or the lightweight Corsair Sabre V2 MG. It goes far beyond just an 8K polling rate; there have been advancements with better battery life, enhanced 2.4GHz wireless stability, and (most crucially) a shift towards a reduction in weight.
Gaming keyboards have come just as far towards the end of 2026 as well. Many of today's decks have embraced the benefits of magnetic sensor technology, through either Hall Effect or TMR, with features such as Rapid Trigger that are genuinely game-changing. It simply dynamically resets a key once your finger lifts up, with an actuation sensitivity as low as 0.1 mm, as opposed to the standard 2mm depth of mechanical decks. Magnets and light sensors also mean fewer moving parts, meaning fewer points of failure — and that leads to a longer lifespan.
I've tested dozens of keyboards over the last 10 months, and (depending on budget), I currently recommend the Logitech G X2 Rapid, Cherry XTRFY K5 Pro TMR, Corsair Clipper Pro Mini 60, and the Razer Huntsman V3 HE 8KHz. You can find more of the best gaming keyboards for around the £100/$100 to $200/£200 mark, depending on whether you want wired or wireless connectivity, and the form factor (essentially, the size of the keyboard and amount of keys).
2. Lean on AI-powered upscaling to boost gaming performance
If one good thing has come out of this whole situation, it's just how far the likes of Nvidia DLSS, AMD FSR, and Intel XeSS have come over the years. All current upscaling methods (DLSS 5, FSR 4, and XeSS 3) render at a lower native resolution and utilize AI to scale the picture up to the target one.
In other words, it means getting playable framerates (60fps or above) in 1440p and even 4K from budget or mid-range graphics cards. This has only gotten better with the implementation of Frame Generation and MFG, which use AI to interpolate generated frames with natively rendered ones, doubling (or tripling) the total framerate in tandem with the resolution bump.
In an ideal world, we would all have the best 4K graphics cards, such as the RTX 5090 and RTX 5080; however, right now Nvidia's flagships are going for as much as $9,000. Given the state of the worldwide economy, that's a hard sell for (almost) everyone on the planet. Luckily, all modern graphics cards from 2020 and upwards (RTX 30 series and RX 5000 line) can make use of this technology, which can help delay the need to upgrade.
It will mean making compromises, though, such as targeting lower resolutions for demanding software, particularly if your current GPU has a smaller memory pool, such as 8GB of GDDR6 or GDDR6X.
3. Push your existing DDR4 or DDR5 RAM to their limits
You may be surprised to hear this, but many PC gamers forget to utilize AMD EXPO or Intel XMP. Whether you've custom-built a rig from scratch or you've purchased a boutique-built or a premade machine from a company like Acer, Alienware, or Corsair, RAM is often set at stock speeds, leaving extra performance off the table. Overclocking RAM is a one-click solution that can make a massive difference to the performance of your PC.
Without EXPO or XMP enabled, DDR4 RAM tops out at 3,200MHz and DDR5 caps at 4,800MHz. This is fine, sure, but you're missing out on anywhere from 20% to 40% of a performance uplift by not enabling this simple BIOS setting, which can see top-end memory modules run at their respective full speeds of 5,333 MHz and 9,600 MHz. Dual-channel RAM, when properly configured, can do more of the heavy lifting with larger games that require additional bandwidth, particularly if they utilize 4K textures, which can exceed upwards of 11GB of VRAM on the GPU.
4. Upgrade to a faster, better gaming monitor
It's easy to forget just how much of a difference one of the best gaming monitors can make to your setup, particularly if you've been used to a slower or duller display.
Panels haven't been subjected to the same price gouging as core components, meaning that the end of 2026 is an ideal time to consider an upgrade. According to the latest Steam Hardware Survey, the bulk of PC gamers are still using 16:9 1080p displays. It's a popular resolution, sure, but 1440p panels have become substantially cheaper and faster, with trusted brands like HP, Gigabyte, and Samsung offering sub-£200/$200 QHD displays, like the Samsung Odyssey G5, Gigabyte G27Q2, and HP Omen 27Q G2, among others.
If you have a little more cash at hand, then you should consider upgrading to either an OLED or a mini-LED gaming monitor. OLED displays have also (thankfully) come down in price, offering (seemingly) unlimited contrast and deep, inky blacks for an unparalleled gaming experience. You can now find top-end displays for as low as $400/£400, such as the Lenovo Legion 27Q-10 OLED, the HyperX Omen OLED, the MSI MAG 271QP QD-OLED, and the Asus ROG Strix OLED XG27AQDMESZ. It really can make a difference to have a brighter, faster, and prettier display to game and work on, even if your hardware doesn't upgrade alongside it.
I'm also the world's biggest cheerleader for 21:9 monitors for both work and play, and these have also come down in price in the last handful of years, too.
Most modern games natively support the ultrawide resolution; it also helps massively if you work from home like me and enjoy juggling more Chrome tabs than is probably healthy. It's a far better way to spend this kind of cash than you would overpaying on a grossly inflated DDR5 RAM kit or a GPU that's double (or triple) its MSRP.
5. Play through your existing gaming backlog instead of newer games
As technology becomes unobtainably expensive and the costs of modern gaming as a hobby continue to skyrocket, it has become a far more viable strategy to look backwards instead of forwards.
While Valve claims that the average Steam user only plays four games a year, that's not a realistic metric for people who primarily game on PC. Take me, for example. I've had a Steam account since 2011, and over the last 15 years, I've accumulated a total of 613 games, or over 900 titles if you count my Steam Family library.
After a quick scan through my games list, I've estimated there are fewer than 100 titles that have any recorded playtime, and only a handful of Steam games that have more than 100 hours invested. I know I'm not alone in this; I am convinced there are thousands of people just like me who see the likes of the Steam Autumn Sale and go on a spending spree, collecting cheap games that will probably never be played.
As such, this tough time for PC gaming is the perfect excuse to finally try to tackle your gaming backlog. In my limited spare time, I'm primarily putting hours into esports games like VALORANT, but when I think about what else to boot up, my mind instantly shifts towards the "Play Next" tab in my Steam library. Steam uses an algorithm to suggest games you should try out based on what you've played before; it knows me to some extent, recommending Assassin's Creed, Half-Life, Splinter Cell, Far Cry, and Sonic the Hedgehog. If you can't afford the cutting edge to keep up with the demanding requirements of modern AAA games, then turning your attention to older, though still great, games should keep you occupied until component prices start to drop.

Formerly TechRadar Gaming's Hardware Editor, Aleksha McLoughlin is now a freelancer specializing in computing tech, gaming, and Ecommerce. She's the author of The Hardest Video Games Ever Made, Head of Kyusai PR, and was the inaugural Editor in Chief of Kyusai.
