Related: New ‘ZeroDayRAT’ Spyware Kit Enables Total Compromise of iOS, Android Devices
articles.summary:
Citizen Lab reports that the Israeli firm Discover-Tech used malicious advertisements to deploy Candiru spyware against Al Jazeera staff, infecting at least 45 devices via zero-click attacks.

### Key Points
- Citizen Lab identified the "AdFection" campaign, which utilized Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform to de-anonymize and infect users through real-time bidding ad auctions.
- Between 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices belonging to Al Jazeera employees were compromised by Candiru spyware.
- Discover-Tech’s infrastructure exposed four billion ad bid records, showing its ads appeared on nearly 200,000 websites and mobile applications.
- Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and Eskimi removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in October following the discovery of these surveillance activities.
- Researchers also linked Discover-Tech to "Dark Cartographer," a group mass-de-anonymizing users by connecting mobile advertising identifiers to private phone numbers.

### Why it Matters
This operation highlights a critical security vulnerability within the global real-time bidding advertising ecosystem, where legitimate ad exchanges can be weaponized to deliver sophisticated spyware. The incident demonstrates how mercenary vendors can bypass traditional defenses to target specific individuals, prompting experts to recommend blocking targeted ads at the network gateway to ensure user safety.

articles.title: North Korean IT Workers Used Stolen US Identities to Earn $3 Million
articles.author: Pierluigi Paganini
articles.content:
The Justice Department (DoJ) announced coordinated enforcement actions this week targeting North Korea’s long-running scheme to place fake IT workers inside American companies. Two US nationals were arrested, 14 people charged across two separate indictments, and the FBI searched more than 40 residences in Texas, seizing approximately 187 laptops and KVM switch devices.
The Texas operation, called Operation Lonestar Roundup, ran between September 21 and 25. The seized devices are the same laptops American companies shipped to their newly hired remote employees, not knowing those IT workers were North Korean intelligence agents using stolen US identities.
“Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through remote information technology (IT) work for U.S. companies.” states DoJ. “These actions include an indictment, two arrests, searches of multiple known or suspected “laptop farms” in Texas pursuant to “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” and the seizure of approximately 187 computer devices used by DPRK IT workers.”
The scheme was simple. North Korean IT workers applied for remote jobs using stolen or fake identities. They used VPNs and proxy servers to make it look like they were working from the United States. American helpers received the laptops provided by employers and installed remote access software so the North Korean workers could use them. These helpers were paid for their role, while the money earned from the jobs was sent back to North Korea through accounts controlled by the regime.
According to an indictment from the Northern District of Ohio, the scheme ran from 2019 to mid-2025 and targeted more than 70 US companies across 17 states. The companies operated in sectors including healthcare, communications, cybersecurity support, retail, and manufacturing.
“In total, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers.” SoJ states.”The revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by the DPRK. Victim employers included companies in the health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio, sixteen additional states, and the District of Columbia.”
The North Korean IT workers earned about $3 million, which prosecutors believe was sent to North Korean entities subject to international sanctions.
The authorities warn the scheme is evolving in response to better detection.
“Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions.” states DoJ. “These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. “
That’s not just using Americans as props. It’s actively outsourcing parts of the operation to people inside the US, which makes attribution harder and interception more complicated.
Some IT workers are now subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. Others are hiring facilitators to handle a wider range of tasks beyond just managing the laptops. CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI investigate, tracks the group behind this operation as Famous Chollima and describes the laptop farm infrastructure as vital to overcoming the physical and legal barriers of operating from outside the US.
“These laptop farms enabled FAMOUS CHOLLIMA operatives to pose as legitimate remote workers and siphon illicit wages back to their regime while maintaining persistent access to victim organizations. Working alongside the FBI, CrowdStrike’s threat intelligence into the adversary and their operations, and technical analysis helped make these disruptions possible.” states CrowdStrike.
“This operation marks the beginning of a broader U.S. law enforcement effort to dismantle FAMOUS CHOLLIMA’s U.S. infrastructure. CrowdStrike’s Counter Adversary Operations team intends to remain an integral part of that effort.”
The FBI’s separate public service announcement puts the operation in broader context: “thousands of North Korean state-controlled IT workers” are currently embedded at Western companies, posing what the agency calls a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat. North Korean IT workers have individually earned up to $300,000 per year under these schemes, and the collective revenue is measured in hundreds of millions annually, flowing directly to designated entities including the North Korean Ministry of Defense.
This is the fifth round of enforcement actions announced since June 2025 under the DOJ’s DPRK RevGen Domestic Enabler Initiative (June 2025, November 2025, April 2026, and May 2026). The initiative targets people in the United States who help North Korean IT workers carry out these schemes.
According to CrowdStrike, North Korean hackers were responsible for about half of all documented hands-on cyber intrusions over the past year. The regime is also targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and open-source software projects. In 2025 alone, North Korean attackers stole at least $2 billion in cryptocurrency.
The DOJ released a list of email addresses used in these operations, including accounts like [email protected] and [email protected], which companies can add to their screening indicators. The FBI’s public service announcement includes detailed mitigation guidance on spotting DPRK IT worker applications. The red flags are consistent: inconsistencies in work history, reluctance to appear on video, requests to redirect laptop deliveries, and payment accounts that route through intermediaries.
“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, IT workers)
articles.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice has charged 14 individuals and seized 187 devices in a crackdown on a North Korean scheme placing fake IT workers into American companies.

### Key Points
- Operation Lonestar Roundup involved FBI searches of over 40 Texas residences used as "laptop farms" to facilitate remote work for North Korean intelligence agents.
- The scheme targeted more than 70 U.S. companies across 17 states, including firms in the healthcare, cybersecurity, and manufacturing sectors.
- North Korean operatives generated approximately $3 million in illicit revenue, which was funneled back to sanctioned entities controlled by the regime.
- The threat group, tracked by CrowdStrike as Famous Chollima, increasingly recruits U.S. facilitators to bypass security measures and subcontract tasks to third-party foreign nationals.
- The DOJ has released specific email indicators and hiring red flags to help employers identify and mitigate the risk of North Korean insider threats.

### Why it Matters
This operation highlights a significant national security risk where foreign intelligence agents exploit remote hiring practices to infiltrate Western corporate networks and siphon funds. Companies must now implement more rigorous identity verification and background screening to prevent state-sponsored actors from gaining persistent access to sensitive intellectual property and internal systems.

articles.title: Why AI Hasn’t Triggered Mass Layoffs — Yet
articles.author: Harvard Gazette
articles.content:
By Sy Boles | Harvard Staff Writer | Harvard Gazette
Artificial intelligence can do some jobs already, but experts say CEOs have good reasons to keep humans on the payroll
If you’re looking for omens of an AI jobs apocalypse, you can certainly find them. News outlets report more layoffs attributed to AI this year than last. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei famously said in 2025 that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. Entry-level job postings have fallen by up to 73 percent in four years, by some counts.
Other data points are more reassuring. Largely buoyed by growth in the healthcare industry, the unemployment rate is hovering around 4.1 percent. For every article announcing AI-related layoffs, another one dismisses it as “AI-washing.” And management consulting firm Accenture says 52 percent of top executives expect AI to increase entry-level hiring, not decrease it.
So how to square the dire forecasts with a job market that still looks mostly normal?
Doug Elmendorf, a Harvard Kennedy School economist and former director of the Congressional Budget Office, says the answer may take patience.
“What we’ve seen so far in the labor market from artificial intelligence has very little predictive power for what we’re going to see in the labor market because of AI in five years, or 10 years, or 15 years,” said Elmendorf, the Lucius N. Littauer Professor of Public Policy and a Harvard University Distinguished Service Professor at HKS.
Along with Karen Dynan, also of the Kennedy School, and Louise Sheiner of the Brookings Institution, this spring Elmendorf wrote a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper that examines four possible scenarios for AI’s impact on the economy. The scenarios range from a moderate boost to GDP with little reduction in the number of workers to much faster GDP growth with persistently high unemployment.
The co-authors cautiously declined to speculate on the relative likelihood of their scenarios. But in an interview, Elmendorf tended toward measured worry about job loss.
“I think it’s very likely that there will be significant job losses from artificial intelligence in the coming couple of decades, but that most — not all, but most — of those people will be able to find new work,” he said.
As a comparison, the co-authors point to the China shock in the early 2000s, when a surge of cheap Chinese exports devastated manufacturing communities across the American Midwest and South. They cite other researchers who estimate that the disruption cost about 1.5 to 2 million total jobs between 2000 and 2007. The authors’ scenario for AI has much larger effects, with 3 million people, or roughly 2 percent of the labor force, out of work at any given time — therefore many millions over the next few decades.
What we’ve seen so far in the labor market from artificial intelligence has very little predictive power for what we’re going to see in the labor market because of AI in five years, or 10 years, or 15 years.
–Doug Elmendorf
According to Joseph Fuller, MBA Class of 1960 Professor of Management Practice at Harvard Business School, much of what’s standing in the way of that large-scale disruption is companies’ clumsy implementation.
In collaboration with industry partner Accenture Research, Fuller developed an AI model that analyzed work tasks for all job categories. They found that as of today, 41 percent of all work tasks can be automated or augmented by AI. But firms aren’t rushing to automate.
Only about one-third of firms’ AI experiments are successful, he said, possibly due to faulty data inputs or employees who don’t know what they’re working with.
“Companies are not training people formally, so employees are basically using it like glorified Google, and they’re not getting much productivity out of it,” said Fuller. “Maybe the boss says, ‘Well, this isn’t as good as I was hoping, I guess we shouldn’t worry too much about this.’”
That’s temporary, Fuller warned. He expects adoption to rise as cheaper, more specialized AI agents arrive.
Eventually, all that stands in the way of AI layoffs may be the C-suite resisting the temptation of the “shiny new object,” according to Raffaella Sadun, Charles E. Wilson Professor of Business Administration at HBS and a principal investigator at the HBS Digital Reskilling Lab.
“For the first time we have a technology that learns, sometimes autonomously, that allows us to have access to expertise that has previously been dispersed,” said Sadun. Executives wonder whether AI can automate away the need to invest in human capital, she added. “I think that’s a tremendous trap, a terrible trap.”
Automating people out of their jobs, Sadun said, trades short-term savings for long-term problems. Human employees’ tacit knowledge — firm-specific context about their market, their role, and their resources — makes them far more valuable than their job descriptions suggest.
At the Digital Reskilling Lab, Sadun and Jorge Tamayo, her co-principal investigator and assistant professor of business administration, work with firms to retrain workers for AI-augmented roles, then test whether the training works.
“At the lab, we see investments in human capital and training as strategic investments, meaning these are things you should do not because you want to be nice or corporate-social-responsibility-compliant, but because knowledge plays an important role in your company, and investment in human capital is part of how you create knowledge,” Sadun said.
Similarly, Fuller works with executives who say a 22-year-old with a freshly minted computer science degree might not offer the same value anymore — but the execs understand they can’t have a senior software engineer without first having a junior one. Fuller helps them reimagine their entry-level job descriptions.
At one large tech company, which he declined to name, Fuller helped executives study senior engineers’ performance reviews to see what was holding them back. Many lacked sales and product management experience.
“So rather than stopping hiring junior software engineers, we changed the job description so those hires are still doing some software engineering, but they’re also getting regular structured introductions to sales and product management,” he said. “We can pre-position what we want 10 years from now by getting them the experience their current bosses didn’t get.”
The entry-level job, Fuller said, may now look like a second or third job would have looked five years ago.
But Elmendorf of HKS doubts that entreaties to protect workers that are not backed by such evidence can beat the profit motive.
“Individual companies are going to be focused on what’s good for their company, and yelling at them to do something different can matter a little bit but it won’t fundamentally change their desire to produce goods and services at the lowest possible cost,” he said. “And for a number of companies, that will mean the use of AI instead of workers for some things.”
That is what the government is for, he said: solving collective-action problems that the market isn’t set up to handle.
In his NBER paper with Dynan and Sheiner, Elmendorf described possible solutions including sprawling changes to the nation’s tax scheme, safety-net programs, and unemployment-insurance system. The authors suggest subsidizing private employment, encouraging shorter work weeks, and expanding worker retraining programs. They also consider the value of a wage insurance program that pays laid-off workers part of the difference between what they made at their previous jobs and their new wages.
“Policymakers should be prepared for much bigger economic changes than we’ve seen so far from AI,” Elmendorf said. “Not because we’re sure those changes will happen, but for the same reason you buy insurance against possible problems in your personal life: It might happen, and you’d rather not be surprised when it does.”

Harvard University experts analyze the long-term labor market impact of artificial intelligence, noting that while current job disruption remains limited, significant workforce displacement may occur within decades.

### Key Points
- Harvard economists estimate AI could eventually displace 3 million workers, potentially exceeding the impact of the early 2000s "China shock" on the U.S. labor market.
- Research from Harvard Business School and Accenture indicates that while 41% of work tasks are currently automatable, only one-third of corporate AI experiments succeed.
- Experts warn that companies often fail to provide formal training, leading employees to use AI tools inefficiently rather than boosting actual productivity.
- Economists suggest that policymakers should prepare for potential labor shifts by reforming tax schemes, unemployment insurance, and worker retraining programs.
- Business leaders are encouraged to view human capital as a strategic asset, as employees possess tacit knowledge that AI cannot currently replicate.

### Why it Matters
The transition toward AI-integrated workflows presents a fundamental challenge to traditional entry-level hiring and long-term workforce development. While companies currently struggle with implementation, the eventual adoption of specialized AI agents may force a significant restructuring of the labor market that requires proactive government intervention.
